answers.answer: Test $H_0:\mu=931$ versus $H_a:\mu>931$. The statistic is $z=(1131-931)/(333/\sqrt{30})\approx3.29$, with one-sided p-value about $0.0005$. Reject $H_0$; there is sufficient evidence that the Massachusetts mean exceeded $\$931$.

a. $z=(10.1-10.3)/(6/\sqrt{500})\approx-0.745$, so the two-sided p-value is about 0.456. Fail to reject $H_0$.

b. The 95% interval is $10.1\pm1.96(6/\sqrt{500})=[9.574,10.626]$ thousand miles.
Test $H_0:\mu=8650$ versus $H_a:\mu>8650$. The statistic is $z=(8950-8650)/(735/\sqrt{42})\approx2.64$, with p-value about 0.0041. Reject $H_0$ at 0.01; there is sufficient evidence of an increase.

Test $H_0:\mu=1520$ versus $H_a:\mu<1520$. With $df=24$, $t=(1505-1520)/(86/\sqrt{25})=-0.872$. The left-tail p-value is about 0.196. Fail to reject $H_0$; there is insufficient evidence that mean life is below 1,520 hours.

Let $H_0:p=0.02$ versus $H_a:p>0.02$. Here $\hat p=11/400=0.0275$ and $\operatorname{SE}_0=\sqrt{0.02(0.98)/400}=0.007$. Thus $z=(0.0275-0.02)/0.007=1.07$, with p-value about 0.142. Fail to reject $H_0$ at 0.05; the observed result is not sufficiently unusual to conclude that the defect rate exceeds 2%.

a. $\hat p=44/60=0.7333$. Under $p_0=0.60$, $\operatorname{SE}=\sqrt{0.6(0.4)/60}=0.06325$, so $z=(0.7333-0.60)/0.06325=2.11$ and p-value $\approx0.0175$. Reject $H_0$; the sample supports a proportion above 60%.

b. Adam's House is a convenience sample, not a random sample of all Harvard students, so the result may suffer selection bias and cannot be generalized reliably.

$\hat p=0.56$, $\operatorname{SE}_0=0.05$, and $z=(0.56-0.50)/0.05=1.20$. The p-value is 0.1151, so fail to reject $H_0$. The sample does not provide sufficient evidence that more than half prefer Diet Pepsi; the claim is not statistically supported.

Let $H_0:p=0.37$ (the failure rate has not improved) and $H_a:p<0.37$ (the failure rate is lower). The statistic is $z=(0.28-0.37)/\sqrt{0.37(0.63)/100}\approx-1.86$, with p-value about 0.031. Since 0.031>0.01, fail to reject $H_0$; at the 1% level there is insufficient evidence that the failure rate improved.

Test $H_0:\mu_R-\mu_D=0$ versus $H_a:\mu_R-\mu_D<0$. Welch's standard error is $\sqrt{1.20^2/50+1.36^2/40}=0.2739$, so $t=(4.35-5.84)/0.2739=-5.44$ with approximately 78.5 degrees of freedom. The one-sided p-value is $2.9\times10^{-7}$, so reject $H_0$; regular-coffee drinkers consume less on average.

Test $H_0:\mu=77$ versus $H_a:\mu>77$. With $df=13$, $t=(81.09-77)/(0.91/\sqrt{14})=16.82$. Since $t_{0.90,13}=1.350$, reject $H_0$; there is strong evidence that the mean lifespan exceeds 77 years.

a. $H_0:\mu\le4.0$ (the company's claim) versus $H_a:\mu>4.0$ (the mean is unsafe).

b. $z=(4.5-4.0)/(1.3/\sqrt{100})=3.846$, with right-tail p-value about $0.000060$. Reject $H_0$ at 0.01; there is strong evidence that the mean exceeds 4.0 ounces.
Test $H_0:\mu=1231$ versus $H_a:\mu<1231$. $z=(1103-1231)/(252/\sqrt{25})=-2.540$, p-value $\approx0.0056$. Reject $H_0$; the Utah mean was significantly below $\$1,231$.
Test $H_0:\mu=500$ versus $H_a:\mu\ne500$. $z=(554-500)/(100/\sqrt{25})=2.70$, p-value $\approx0.0069$. Reject at both 0.05 and 0.01; there is evidence of a change, with the observed mean higher.
Test $H_0:\mu=109$ versus $H_a:\mu>109$. $z=(116-109)/(15/\sqrt{122})\approx5.16$, p-value $\approx1.3\times10^{-7}$. Reject $H_0$; UIC students have significantly higher mean IQ.
Test $H_0:\mu=9450$ versus $H_a:\mu>9450$. $z=(9850-9450)/(1035/\sqrt{47})=2.648$, p-value $\approx0.0040$. Reject $H_0$; there is sufficient evidence of an increase.
Test $H_0:\mu=9450$ versus $H_a:\mu>9450$. With $df=24$, $t=(9850-9450)/(1035/\sqrt{25})=1.932$, p-value $\approx0.0326$. Fail to reject at 0.01; evidence is insufficient at that strict level.
Test $H_0:\mu=1520$ versus $H_a:\mu<1520$. With $df=39$, $t=(1505-1520)/(86/\sqrt{40})=-1.103$, p-value $\approx0.138$. Fail to reject $H_0$; there is insufficient evidence of a lower mean life.

a. $t=(23.1-15.3)/(7.2/\sqrt{50})=7.66$ with $df=49$, p-value about $6.3\times10^{-10}$. Reject $H_0$; the means differ.

b. With $t_{0.975,49}=2.010$, the interval is $23.1\pm2.046=[21.054,25.146]$ thousand miles.

Test $H_0:\mu=200$ versus $H_a:\mu\ne200$. Since $s=\sqrt{300}=17.3205$, $t=(221-200)/(17.3205/\sqrt{14})=4.537$ with $df=13$. The two-sided p-value is about 0.00056. Reject $H_0$; the medication changes the mean, with an observed increase.
Test $H_0:\mu=110.3$ versus $H_a:\mu\ne110.3$. With $s=18$ and $df=35$, $t=(114.5-110.3)/(18/\sqrt{36})=1.40$, p-value $\approx0.170$. Fail to reject $H_0$; evidence of a difference is insufficient.
Test $H_0:p=0.50$ versus $H_a:p>0.50$. $\hat p=0.56$, null SE $=0.05$, so $z=1.20$ and p-value $=0.1151$. Fail to reject $H_0$; evidence is insufficient that more than half prefer Diet Coke.

Test $H_0:p=0.90$ versus $H_a:p<0.90$. $\hat p=103/122=0.8443$, null SE $=\sqrt{0.9(0.1)/122}=0.02716$, and $z=-2.05$. The p-value is about 0.0201, so reject $H_0$; the data suggest the recovery rate is below 90%.

Let $d=\text{Before}-\text{After}$, giving $2,0,-1,4,4,3,0,8$. Then $\bar d=2.5$, $s_d=2.9277$, and $t=2.415$ with $df=7$ for $H_0:\mu_d=0$ versus $H_a:\mu_d>0$. The one-sided p-value is about 0.0232, so reject $H_0$; the modification significantly reduces mean accidents.
